prompt: You need to point `example.com`, without `www`, at a hosted service that only gives you a name (`app.provider.net`) and no IP. Why does a `CNAME` not solve it?
hint: `CNAME` has a restriction on its position in the domain. Where exactly can it not exist, and which records already occupy that place?

choices.text: A `CNAME` cannot exist at the domain root, which has to coexist with other records such as the `MX`.
choices.why: The way out is `A` with fixed IPs, or an `ALIAS`/`ANAME`, a non-standard extension some providers offer.

choices.text: A `CNAME` only works for third-level subdomains or deeper.
choices.why: It works on any name that is not the root — `www.example.com` is second level and is accepted.

choices.text: A `CNAME` requires the target to be in the same domain as the name pointing at it.
choices.why: The target can be any name, including one belonging to another organisation.

choices.text: `CNAME` was deprecated in favour of `ALIAS` and is no longer honoured by resolvers.
choices.why: It is still in full use; it is `ALIAS` that is the non-standard extension.

prompt: Put the steps of a server migration in order, so that no visitor lands on a dead address.
hint: One of the steps has to happen well before the others for the rest to take effect quickly. Which of them depends on what the caches have already kept?
items: Lower the record's TTL to a few minutes, a day before the switch
Bring the application up on the new server and confirm it answers on its IP
Change the record to point at the new address
Confirm that the traffic is reaching the new server
Put the TTL back up to hours
trap: The lower-the-TTL–change-the-record pair. It is tempting to lower the TTL along with the change, or after it, to "speed up propagation". It does not work: the ceiling on the wait is the TTL that was already in force when the caches kept the old answer. Lowering it afterwards only affects the following queries, and the switch still takes the whole old TTL.
